items.title: Pre-employment checks (BPSS)
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Every Civil Service job offer depends on pre-employment checks. The minimum set is the Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS). It confirms your identity, your nationality and right to work in the UK, your employment history (usually for the past three years) and any unspent criminal convictions. You will be asked for original documents and the details of previous employers or others who can confirm what you were doing. If you were not working, for example because you were caring for children, you will be asked to explain how you spent the time and may need someone who can confirm it. Honesty is essential: leaving something out or giving wrong information can lead to an offer being withdrawn, even if the original fact would not have mattered.

questions.prompt: What is the Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS)?

options.text: A set of basic pre-employment checks used for people joining government

questions.prompt: Which of these is checked under the BPSS?

options.text: Identity, right to work, recent employment history and unspent criminal convictions

questions.prompt: You were at home caring for children for the last three years. What should you do when asked about your recent history?

options.text: Explain it honestly and be ready to give someone who can confirm it
Leave it blank and say nothing

questions.prompt: After accepting an offer you realise you left a short job off your employment history. What should you do?
questions.answer: Tell the recruitment team promptly and give the correct information, before it is discovered. Honest correction is far better than an omission found later, which can lead to the offer being withdrawn because of the lack of honesty. Explain simply that you made an oversight, supply the details and keep copies of what you send.
questions.rubric: Should say to tell the recruiters promptly, correct the record honestly, and recognise omission is a risk to the offer.

items.title: Nationality and right to work
items.body: To work in the Civil Service you must have the right to work in the UK. Nationality rules decide which jobs you can do. Many Civil Service jobs are open to UK nationals and also to citizens of some other countries and people with certain immigration permissions. Some jobs, for example those involving national security, are reserved for UK nationals only, or for those with a specific status. Each advert has an eligibility statement saying who can apply. Read it before you start. If you are unsure, use the contact in the advert. Do not guess and do not assume your situation is the same as someone else's: rules depend on your own status.

questions.prompt: What do you usually need to show to prove you may work in the UK?

options.text: Documents confirming your right to work

questions.prompt: Where would you find out whether a job is restricted to UK nationals?

options.text: After you have been offered the job
In the eligibility or nationality statement in the advert

questions.prompt: What should you do before applying if you are unsure whether you are eligible?

options.text: Check the advert's eligibility information and ask the recruitment contact
Ask a stranger online and rely on the answer

questions.prompt: You have settled status in the UK and want to apply for an AO role, but you are unsure whether you are eligible. What steps do you take?
questions.answer: Read the eligibility and nationality section in the advert carefully. Check the Civil Service nationality guidance on GOV.UK, then contact the named recruitment contact before the closing date to confirm your situation, describing it accurately. Keep your documents ready, such as proof of status and identity. Do not rely on hearsay and do not apply for a restricted role that you cannot hold.
questions.rubric: Should read the advert, check GOV.UK guidance, contact the recruiters before closing, and have documents ready.

items.title: Security clearance levels
items.body: Beyond the BPSS, some roles need security clearance. The main levels are Counter-Terrorist Check (CTC), Security Check (SC) and Developed Vetting (DV), each more detailed than the one before. SC and DV usually expect a minimum period of residence in the UK, often about five years for SC and longer for DV, and involve checks on your background, finances and sometimes family. Many entry-level roles need only BPSS, but jobs in sensitive areas may need higher clearance. The advert states the level needed and clearance takes time, sometimes months. An advert that needs clearance you cannot get is not for you right now, but there may be many others that are.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the highest level of security clearance?
SC clearance usually expects how long of residence in the UK?
Which statement about clearance for entry roles is most accurate?

options.text: Every entry role needs Developed Vetting
Clearance is decided only on the first day
Many entry roles need only BPSS, but the advert states the level

questions.prompt: An advert says the role needs SC clearance. You have lived abroad for three of the last five years. What do you do?
questions.answer: Read the advert's guidance on residence and clearance, then contact the recruitment team before applying to explain your situation and ask whether it would affect eligibility. Do not assume the answer either way. If it would, look for roles that need only BPSS in the meantime and plan to apply for the SC role once you meet the residence guidance.
questions.rubric: Should read the guidance, contact recruiters before applying, not assume, and consider other roles meanwhile.

items.title: Joining and the first weeks
items.body: Once your checks are cleared you receive a confirmed start date and a contract. Your first days include an induction: meeting your line manager and team, getting your equipment and pass, and learning how the department works. You will complete mandatory learning, for example on security, data protection, equality and the Civil Service Code. Ask questions: nobody expects a new starter to know everything. Keep personal and customer information confidential, and follow the rules about what you may share and where. You will usually agree objectives with your manager and have regular one-to-ones. Look out for a buddy or mentor and use training and development offers to prepare for promotion.

options.text: An introduction to the job, the team and the department when you start

questions.prompt: Why must civil servants handle customer information carefully?

options.text: Because the information is public anyway
It is confidential and protected by law and by the Civil Service Code
It is only a matter of politeness

questions.prompt: What is the best attitude to questions in your first weeks?

options.text: Never ask, so you look capable
Ask questions early, because nobody expects a new starter to know everything

questions.prompt: Plan your first two weeks as a new Administrative Officer so you settle in well and make a good impression.
questions.answer: Week 1: meet your manager and team, ask about your objectives and what a good first month looks like, complete mandatory learning on security and data protection, learn the main systems and procedures, and find out who to ask for help. Week 2: start work on real cases under guidance, check your work carefully, ask for feedback, keep notes of what you learn and agree a regular one-to-one. Be punctual, reliable and friendly, and follow the confidentiality and security rules from the first day.
questions.rubric: Should include meeting the manager, objectives, mandatory learning, asking questions, feedback and following security rules.
